name: Measuring the World: Units, Scales and Standards
description: From the cubit to the SI: how people agreed on lengths, weights and temperatures, mapped the Earth, and built the instruments that made precise measurement possible.

checkpoints.name: Body and sky
checkpoints.note: Early measures came from the body, like the cubit, the length of a forearm, and Babylonian counting in sixties gave the degree its minutes and seconds. Ptolemy mapped the known world with latitude and longitude, and portolan charts drew the coasts of the Mediterranean.

checkpoints.name: The age of instruments
checkpoints.note: Astronomers and surveyors measured angles with the Jacob's staff, the thermometer and the barometer gave numbers to heat and air pressure, and the microscope revealed tiny things. Logarithms and the slide rule eased calculation, Daniel Fahrenheit made a reliable mercury thermometer and scale, and Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742.

checkpoints.name: Standards for a new age
checkpoints.note: After the French Revolution the metric system offered a common standard based on the size of the Earth, while Britain fixed its imperial units in 1824. Lord Kelvin set out an absolute scale of temperature, nations chose a prime meridian for the world's maps in 1884, and the National Geographic Society was founded in 1888.

checkpoints.name: Precision from the atom
checkpoints.note: The Geiger counter measured radiation, and the International System of Units of 1960 gave the world one set of units, which in 2019 were tied to fixed constants of nature. LIGO now measures changes in length far smaller than an atom.
